23:1.text: But before all these, they shall lay their hands on you, and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues, and into prisons, being brought before kings and rulers for my name’s sake.

provenance.other: “lay their hands on you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 21:12. The Book of Mormon has the phrase twice in two verses (23:1, 23:2) with the object changed from 'you' to the named missionaries, and it keeps Luke's third-person plural subject — the persecutors, not the prisoners.
provenance.significance: Luke 21:12 is Jesus telling his disciples what will be done to them: hands laid on them, delivered to synagogues, into prisons, brought before kings. Alma 23:1-2 is a king cancelling that list item by item, and the cancellation is issued from the one position in Luke's sentence that is not a victim's. The metalepsis is in the last clause of the source, 'for my name's sake': in Luke the king before whom the preacher is brought is the persecution's final stage, and here the king is the reason the preaching is safe. The Book of Mormon has taken the standard KJV catalogue of what happens to missionaries and made a royal decree out of its negation.

23:1.note: 'The king of the Lamanites sent a proclamation among all his people, that they should not lay their hands on Ammon, or Aaron, or Omner, or Himni, nor neither of their brethren which should go forth preaching the word of God.' 'Lay their hands on you' is Luke 21:12's alone in the KJV, and Luke 21:12 is the verse that assembles the whole apparatus this proclamation dismantles — hands, synagogues, prisons, kings. Mark 13:9 is the synoptic parallel and contributes the beating that Alma 23:2 also forbids. Note that the 1830's 'nor neither of their brethren' is a double negative the 1920 edition repairs to 'either'; the first edition's construction is not the KJV's here, and the borrowing is in the clause before it.

23:2.text: But beware of men: for they will deliver you up to the councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues;

provenance.route: Matthew 10:17 (with John 16:2, Matthew 23:34) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Four of the decree's seven prohibitions are KJV singletons or near it. “scourge you in their synagogues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 10:17; “put you out of the synagogues” in exactly one, John 16:2; “in the synagogues ye shall be beaten” in exactly one, Mark 13:9. Spitting on a messenger is Mark 10:34's and Luke 18:32's; stoning one is Mark 12:4's, where the husbandmen 'cast stones' at the servant sent to them; binding and imprisoning is Acts 5:18, where the council 'laid their hands on the apostles, and put them in the common prison'. The pronoun is worth catching by eye: Matthew 23:34 has Jesus tell his hearers 'ye shall scourge in YOUR synagogues', and Matthew 10:17 tells the disciples 'they will scourge you in THEIR synagogues'. The Book of Mormon's 'nor cast them out of their synagogues' has Matthew 10:17's grammar, which is the correct one for a decree addressed to the persecutors about their own buildings.
provenance.significance: The list is not a list of things that might happen; it is the King James Bible's list, negated. Every item the decree forbids is an item the gospels promise will be done to a preacher, and they are assembled from the two discourses where Jesus tells his messengers what to expect (Matthew 10, Mark 13 / Luke 21) plus the passion predictions where the same is done to him. Recover those contexts and the decree reads as an answer to a prophecy: what Jesus says his messengers must endure, this king makes it illegal to do. The last item is the tell — 'but that they should have free access to their houses, and also their temples, and their sanctuaries' — because access to the synagogue is exactly what John 16:2 says will be withdrawn.

23:2.note: 'That they should not lay their hands on them to bind them, or to cast them into prison; neither should they spit upon them, nor smite them, nor cast them out of their synagogues, nor scourge them; neither should they cast stones at them.' Seven prohibitions, and each one names a specific KJV persecution rather than a general cruelty: scourging in synagogues (Matthew 10:17, a singleton), expulsion from synagogues (John 16:2, a singleton), beating in synagogues (Mark 13:9, a singleton), spitting and smiting (Mark 10:34), stoning a sent servant (Mark 12:4), binding and imprisonment (Acts 5:18). Matthew 10:17 is given as the source because it holds the two elements the Book of Mormon keeps together, the scourging and the synagogue, and because its pronoun is the one the Book of Mormon uses. No clause is reproduced entire and this falls well below Skousen's threshold for a quotation; what makes the case is that a seven-item list should be drawn item by item from one narrow band of the KJV.

23:3.text: He saith unto him, Which? Jesus said, Thou shalt do no murder, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness,

provenance.mt: Exodus 20:13-15, 'Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal.'
provenance.route: Exodus 20:13-15 → Matthew 19:18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The whole decision rests on one word. “do no murder” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 19:18; every other KJV form of the sixth commandment — Exodus 20:13, Deuteronomy 5:17, Mark 10:19, Luke 18:20, Romans 13:9, James 2:11 — reads 'kill'. Alma 23:3 reads 'murder', and it reads it first in the list, which is Matthew 19:18's order and not Mark 10:19's or Exodus's. tools/mediation-check.py returns Matthew 19:18 as decisive, though on a crude whole-verse diff; the human ground is the single word 'murder' and the position it holds.
provenance.significance: Matthew 19:18 is the answer given to the rich young ruler when he asks 'Which?' — and Alma 22:15 has already put that same ruler's question in this king's mouth, in Matthew 19:16's own words. So the two halves of one gospel pericope are distributed across two Book of Mormon chapters and given to one man: at 22:15 he asks what he must do for eternal life and offers his kingdom, and at 23:3 he proclaims to his people the commandments Jesus answered that question with. The fourth item is the one that does not come from Matthew — 'nor to plunder' — and it is what the list has to add for a people whose sin the book has been describing since Alma 17 as robbery. Mark 10:19 ends its own version of the list with 'Defraud not', which is the KJV's nearest word for it.

23:3.note: 'They had not ought to murder, nor to plunder, nor to steal, nor to commit adultery, nor to commit any manner of wickedness.' A four-item decalogue, and the mediation is settled by its first word: the KJV says 'kill' everywhere in this commandment except Matthew 19:18, which says 'do no murder', and the Book of Mormon says murder. Matthew 19:18 also puts murder first, where Mark 10:19 and Luke 18:20 begin with adultery and Exodus's numbering is not a list at all. That the source should be Matthew 19:18 specifically is not incidental: Alma 22:15 borrowed Matthew 19:16, the question this verse answers. The 1830's 'had not ought to' is the first edition's; 1920 regularizes it to 'ought not to', which loses nothing of the borrowing but is worth recording as the running text's own idiom rather than the KJV's.

23:7.text: But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God.

provenance.other: “fight against God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 5:39 and Acts 23:9, and both are a Pharisee counselling a council against acting on apostles in its custody. The Book of Mormon's clause is the phrase in Gamaliel's form, negated and made a description of converts: 'they did not fight against God no more' (1830; 1920 repairs the double negative to 'any more').
provenance.significance: The whole of Acts 5:17-42 is standing behind Alma 23. Acts 5:18 is the council laying hands on the apostles and putting them in prison, which Alma 23:1-2 forbids by decree; Acts 5:38-39 is Gamaliel telling that council to refrain from these men and let them alone, because if the work is of God it cannot be overthrown and they would be found fighting against God; Acts 5:40 is the council beating them and commanding them not to preach. Alma 23 is Gamaliel's counsel actually taken — a ruler who lets the men alone, on the ground that their work is of God — and 23:3's clause that 'the word of God might have no obstruction' is Acts 5:39's 'ye cannot overthrow it' from the other side. Acts 5 has already been read into this book at Alma 2:2, where Gamaliel's Theudas supplies the shape of Amlici; the phrase itself has not been used before Alma 23:7.

23:7.note: 'They did lay down the weapons of their rebellion, that they did not fight against God no more, neither against any of their brethren.' 'Fight against God' is a KJV phrase of exactly two verses, both in Acts, both spoken by a Pharisee restraining a council from destroying preachers it has arrested — and Alma 23 has just described a ruler doing precisely that restraining. The converts here are not merely people who stopped fighting Nephites; the word chosen for what they stopped doing is Gamaliel's word for what a court does when it acts against apostles. Alma 2:2 has already used Gamaliel's speech for its Theudas; this is the phrase from its climax, and the chapter around it is the counsel obeyed.

23:17.text: And they said unto her, There is none of thy kindred that is called by this name.

provenance.other: “called by this name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:61. “called by a new name” occurs in exactly one, Isaiah 62:2. Acts 11:26, the disciples 'called Christians first in Antioch', is the KJV's only narrative of a body of converts acquiring a distinguishing name, and it shares no wording with Alma 23:17.
provenance.significance: Luke 1:61 is an objection, and the objection is about kindred: 'There is none of thy kindred that is called by this name.' The naming of John the Baptist is the KJV's one scene in which a family's naming convention is deliberately broken, and the breaking is at God's instruction and marks the child off from his relations. Alma 23:16-17 is a people asking for a name 'that thereby they might be distinguished from their brethren', receiving one, and being 'no more called Lamanites' — a naming whose whole point is the severance from kindred that Luke 1:61 objects to. Isaiah 62:2's promised new name is the theological warrant a reader will reach for first; Luke 1:61 is where the KJV's actual words are.

23:17.note: 'They called their name Anti-Nephi-Lehies; and they were called by this name, and were no more called Lamanites.' The phrase 'called by this name' occurs once in the KJV, in the neighbours' protest at John's naming, and its subject there is exactly the subject here: a name that does not belong to the kindred. This is recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because four common words are all the verbal contact there is, and because the naming of a convert people has two better-known scriptural warrants — Isaiah 62:2's new name and Acts 11:26's Christians — neither of which supplies any wording.
23:17.whyNot: 'Called by this name' is a phrase four ordinary words long, and its being a KJV singleton may be an accident of a common construction rather than evidence of borrowing. A reader who finds Isaiah 62:2 and Acts 11:26 sufficient to explain the scene, and the wording unremarkable, is not being unreasonable.
